What is the critical path method and how do you use it to manage complex projects?

Critical Path Method (CPM): identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks in a project — this sequence determines the minimum project duration. Any delay on the critical path delays the entire project. Construction: 1) List all tasks and their durations. 2) Identify dependencies (which tasks must complete before others start). 3) Draw network diagram (Activity on Node). 4) Calculate Early Start (ES) and Early Finish (EF) with forward pass: ES = max(EF of all predecessors). EF = ES + Duration. 5) Late Start (LS) and Late Finish (LF) with backward pass: LF = min(LS of all successors). LS = LF - Duration. 6) Float/Slack = LS - ES. Tasks with zero float are on critical path. Application: focus management attention on critical path tasks — that's where delays hurt. Use float strategically — can delay non-critical tasks to level resource demand. Compression techniques: Crashing (add resources to critical path tasks — reduces duration at cost). Fast-tracking (run normally sequential critical path tasks in parallel — increases risk). Modern adaptation: critical chain project management (Goldratt) adds buffer management and addresses student syndrome (procrastination) and Parkinson's law (work expands to fill time).

How do you run effective retrospectives that actually improve team performance?

Retrospectives fail when they become complaint sessions with no action or when psychological safety is insufficient for honest feedback. Effective format: Prime Directive (Norm Kerth): 'Regardless of what we discover, we understand that everyone did the best job they could given what they knew at the time.' Removes blame, enables learning. Structure (Sailboat retrospective): Wind (what moves us forward — what's working), Anchor (what slows us down), Rocks (risks ahead), Sun/Island (goal we're heading toward). Each person writes on sticky notes independently before discussion — prevents anchoring bias from dominant voices. Dot voting to prioritize. Action items: maximum 3, each with owner and due date, reviewed at next retro. For deeper issues: 5 Whys applied to identified problems — typically reveals process or systemic issues underneath surface symptoms. Safety check: anonymous survey (1-5 scale 'How safe do you feel speaking openly?') before starting. If average < 3, facilitator problem — address psychological safety before content. Liberating structures: 1-2-4-ALL (individual reflection → pairs → groups of 4 → whole group) ensures quieter voices. Review previous action items first — nothing kills retro credibility faster than ignored previous actions.

How do elite teams handle failure and what separates learning organizations from non-learning ones?

Learning organization characteristics (Senge): Systems thinking, personal mastery, mental model examination, shared vision, team learning. Failure response in high-reliability organizations (HROs — aviation, nuclear, military special operations): Blameless post-mortems: find systemic causes, not human villains. The same human in the same system conditions will make the same error — fix the system. Near-miss reporting: HROs actively encourage reporting near-misses because they're free information about system vulnerabilities. Organizations with blame cultures suppress near-miss reporting — first warning becomes the accident. After Action Review (AAR) format: What was intended? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently? Four categories: sustain (what worked), improve (what failed), start (what was missing), stop (what was counterproductive). Psychological safety (Amy Edmondson): the #1 predictor of team learning and performance. Team members must believe they can raise concerns without punishment. Google Project Aristotle found psychological safety the top predictor of team effectiveness. Non-learning organization signals: post-mortems that end in individual blame, issues raised in private but not in meetings, cover-up of failures, no mechanism for bottom-up information flow.
